title: The Small Suffer What They Must?
gist: Long and Patrick argue the erosion of restraints on great-power behavior — average U.S. tariffs up from under 3 percent to 13.7 percent, a paralyzed WTO, aid down nearly a quarter in 2025, and open threats to Panama, Greenland, Canada and Venezuela — is transferring risk onto small and medium states that lack the tools to shape rules. Their prescription is collective action through one-state-one-vote bodies, niche diplomatic specialization, below-the-radar hedging, and hard-nosed transactional bargaining over chokepoints and critical minerals.

themes.theme: Great-power predation as the new baseline

insights.claim: The menacing of small and medium-sized states accelerated sharply in 2026 with a raid to remove Venezuela's president and an oil blockade of Cuba, following January 2025 pledges to take back the Panama Canal and acquire Greenland.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: Territorial and regime-change coercion against small states is now demonstrated policy, not rhetoric — a persistent political risk premium for frontier sovereign debt and commodity assets in the Western Hemisphere.
insights.locator: Since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to office

insights.claim: Erosion of restraints on great-power behavior is not a U.S.-only phenomenon: Russia's invasion of Ukraine and China's expansionism in the South China Sea mean there are now vanishingly few checks on intervention and conquest.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: Systemic, not partisan: the norm decay persists through U.S. political cycles, so hedges against territorial-risk events should be structural rather than event-driven.
insights.locator: The president’s might-makes-right approach

insights.claim: The global norm against aggression is at its weakest since World War II, with the United States issuing threats and conducting military actions without even a nod to international law — including kidnapping a head of state in Venezuela and helping kill another in Iran without any pretense of legality.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: If legality no longer constrains, expropriation and regime-change scenarios must be priced into any asset whose value depends on a small state's sovereign continuity.
insights.quote: Meanwhile, the global norm against aggression is at its weakest since World War II.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, the global norm against aggression

insights.claim: Since Trump's return, the United States has threatened the sovereignty of Canada and the territorial integrity or inviolability of Colombia, Mexico, Panama and Denmark via Greenland — while Israel operates unrestrained in Gaza and Lebanon and Pakistan wages an 'open war' against Afghanistan without repercussion.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: The contagion of unpunished aggression widens the set of geographies where cross-border escalation is plausible, which matters for defense demand and regional currency risk.
insights.locator: Since Trump’s return to the White House

themes.theme: Coercion has a cost curve for the strong

insights.claim: Coercion has already produced concrete commercial wins for Washington: pressure drove Panama to review Chinese-linked port operators near the canal, and Venezuela's newly U.S.-backed leadership opened the country's oil industry to U.S. companies.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: Coercion is generating real asset transfers — U.S. oil and port operators are direct beneficiaries, and Chinese-linked infrastructure operators face forced divestment risk.
insights.locator: Big powers may bully their way to success

insights.claim: Sustaining coercion is expensive and risks miring the strong in the affairs of the weak, and as in Cuba it can produce social and economic catastrophe with no clear political endgame — putting great powers on a slippery slope toward increasingly costly interventions.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: Coercion wins are front-loaded and costs back-loaded, so early 'success' headlines are a poor guide to the fiscal and escalation bill that follows.
insights.quote: But sustaining coercion is expensive and risks miring the strong in the affairs of the weak.
insights.locator: But sustaining coercion is expensive

insights.claim: The global public goods the United States provided were never charity but a winning wager that a relatively stable and open system would underpin U.S. alliances, partnerships and prosperity, and a superpower that roils the waters around smaller states will find the waves reach its own shores.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: Frames aid and institution-funding cuts as negative-return trades for the U.S. itself — the blowback channel runs through value chains, financial hubs, chokepoints and basing access.
insights.quote: Ultimately, a superpower that roils the waters around smaller states will find that the waves reach its own shores.
insights.locator: The global public goods the United States provided

insights.claim: Smaller states retain real strategic value to great powers because they are woven into global value chains, serve as financial hubs, act as strategic chokepoints and offer basing opportunities — leverage sharpened by U.S.-China competition in which Beijing assiduously courts the broader UN membership.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: Small-state leverage is not zero — chokepoint and minerals-holding states can extract terms, which is the tradable side of this dynamic.
insights.locator: Smaller states are woven into global value chains

themes.theme: What the postwar order actually bought small states

insights.claim: UN membership more than tripled from 51 to 159 by the 1980s and surged to 193 after the Cold War, so most members are small and medium-sized states — the very countries now facing the greatest pressure from intersecting global crises.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: The numerical majority of the UN is now the constituency most exposed to order breakdown, which explains why one-state-one-vote bodies become the natural battleground.
insights.locator: THE ORDER THAT WAS

insights.claim: International law functioned as the practical defense mechanism of weak states by compelling aggressors to justify rule breaches, captured in former Estonian President Lennart Meri's line that international law is the nuclear weapon of small states.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: If the justification requirement disappears, the sole deterrent small states possessed is gone — a step-change in expropriation and invasion risk rather than a gradual drift.
insights.quote: The nuclear weapon of small states is international law.
insights.locator: As former Estonian President Lennart Meri quipped

insights.claim: In an open world economy very small states found niches and grew wealthier on average than larger counterparts — Qatar invested heavily to become an LNG exporter, global investor and regional hub, achievements now at risk, while Chile diversified under trade-institution protection only to be pressured by Washington to pick sides against China.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: Niche-specialist economies built on open trade — LNG exporters, commodity diversifiers, financial hubs — carry the most fragmentation downside as bloc pressure forces alignment.
insights.locator: The postwar international order also provided openness and predictability

insights.claim: Small states organized their own leverage structures inside the UN system, including the UN Forum on Small States with roughly 108 members, and produced concrete outcomes such as the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons and the International Court of Justice's climate advisory opinion spearheaded by tiny Vanuatu.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: Small-state coalitions have a track record of moving legal and normative outcomes — the ICJ climate opinion channel is a live source of litigation risk for emitters.
insights.locator: International organizations cushioned smaller states

insights.claim: The average U.S. tariff rate has surged from less than three percent to 13.7 percent, with some states hit by far higher, crippling fees.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: A better-than-fourfold rise in the average applied tariff is a durable input-cost and margin variable for import-dependent supply chains, not a temporary negotiating posture.
insights.quote: The average U.S. tariff rate has surged from less than three percent to 13.7 percent
insights.locator: Today, smaller states confront imposing economic barriers

insights.claim: Lesotho, with GDP per capita of about $1,000, was hit with 50 percent U.S. tariffs on its denim industry in April 2025, prompting factory freezes and layoffs among a vulnerable, largely female workforce.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: Shows tariff policy can wipe out a single-sector low-income economy overnight — apparel sourcing risk in AGOA-type geographies should be treated as binary.
insights.locator: One is Lesotho, a country with a GDP per capita of about $1,000

insights.claim: The WTO has been neutered by great-power discord and U.S. steps to paralyze its dispute-resolution body, including blocking appointment of new appellate judges, leaving aggrieved trading nations with no forum to plead their case.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: With no binding adjudication, tariff actions are effectively unappealable — trade risk becomes a pure function of bilateral political leverage.
insights.locator: In the past, aggrieved trading nations could have pleaded their case

insights.claim: Official development aid plummeted by nearly a quarter in 2025 and is still falling as the United States and other donors pull back sharply, while Washington has slashed political and financial support for international organizations.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: A ~25 percent aid contraction removes fiscal buffers for aid-dependent sovereigns — raises default and instability risk in small-island and low-income credits.
insights.locator: Many of the global public goods that smaller states have long relied on

insights.claim: Small-island developing countries are triply threatened by climate inaction, broken storm-warning systems and diminished disaster-relief funds, after global monitoring systems anchored by U.S. scientific agencies had previously provided early warning of diseases, extreme weather and storms.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: Loss of public early-warning infrastructure raises realized catastrophe losses — relevant to catastrophe reinsurance pricing and sovereign cat-bond structuring.
insights.locator: The costs are clearest for small-island developing countries

insights.claim: The United States, China and other powers are likely to link international loans to commodity collateral, consistent with Beijing's lending practices and U.S. supervision of post-Maduro Venezuela's oil industry, further impinging on smaller states' autonomy.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: Commodity-collateralized sovereign lending is the emerging template — it subordinates existing bondholders' claims on resource revenue and reshapes recovery assumptions.
insights.locator: Going forward, the United States, China, and other powers are likely to link

insights.claim: Governance innovations touted as broadening representation, such as BRICS expanding from five founding members to 11, have troubling implications for smaller states because decision-making power shifts from the universal UN system to exclusive minilateral frameworks that leave them out.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: A contrarian read on BRICS expansion: it concentrates rather than democratizes power, so expect small-state resistance rather than automatic Global South alignment.
insights.locator: Even some global governance innovations touted as enlarging representation

insights.claim: Middle-power diplomacy advocated by Canada, Indonesia and Turkey cuts both ways: it may offer an alternative to great-power dominance but these coalitions may still ignore or even bully smaller countries.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: Middle-power blocs are not a reliable protective layer — do not assume they will absorb small-state interests when modeling coalition behavior.
insights.locator: Likewise, the middle-power diplomacy now advocated

insights.claim: Trump's disruption and unpredictability makes global markets swing daily, forcing smaller states to navigate constant turbulence while great-power competition drives small-country defections and side deals that yield short-term protection but weaken the more beneficial system over time.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: Policy-driven daily volatility is itself the regime — favors volatility-tolerant positioning and penalizes small-state carry trades that assume stability.
insights.quote: Acting as a “predatory hegemon,” as Stephen M. Walt described in these pages, a rogue United States now discards rules and institutions that do not serve its immediate ends.
insights.locator: VANISHING CERTAINTIES

themes.theme: The small-state playbook: collective action, niche, hedging, deals

insights.claim: Smaller states should boost contributions to international organizations to offset U.S. cuts, which rising incomes over recent decades have made affordable for countries beyond the great powers.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: Watch for non-great-power funding of multilateral bodies as a signal of which institutions survive the U.S. withdrawal — a determinant of aid and standards continuity.
insights.quote: if they do not hang together, they will surely hang separately
insights.locator: HANG TOGETHER

insights.claim: Concrete small-state accountability mechanisms already exist and can be scaled, including the 2022 UN General Assembly 'veto initiative' led by the microstate Liechtenstein requiring permanent Security Council members to publicly justify vetoes, and the 39-country Alliance of Small Island States that has shaped multilateral climate negotiations for three decades.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: Coalition mechanics in climate talks let small states punch far above economic weight — a real driver of transition-policy outcomes affecting energy assets.
insights.locator: Working collectively—particularly through one-state, one-vote bodies

insights.claim: Small states must specialize and exercise niche leadership because most cannot maintain global embassy networks or staff every UN body, with the Organisation of Eastern Caribbean States pooling resources for joint representation abroad as a replicable model.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: Pooled diplomatic capacity is the low-cost lever — watch for more sub-regional bodies as negotiating agents, which changes who counterparties actually deal with.
insights.locator: Smaller states must also improve their diplomatic capacities

insights.claim: Western Hemisphere countries that responded to Trump's dominance by immediately aligning with Washington are pursuing a self-defeating strategy that deepens dependence, whereas diversifying intra- and cross-regional partnerships below the radar of a mercurial hegemon and pursuing multialignment increases leverage.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: Against the consensus bandwagoning trade: the authors expect quiet diversification to outperform alignment, implying gradual erosion of U.S. commercial exclusivity in the hemisphere.
insights.quote: ideally below the radar of a mercurial hegemon
insights.locator: Additionally, smaller states will have to get better at hedging

insights.claim: ASEAN has turned U.S.-Chinese competition to its own advantage through the ASEAN Plus Three forum, where it sets the agenda for joint meetings with China, Japan and South Korea, and led creation of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership bringing fifteen Asian and Oceanic economies into the world's largest free trade agreement.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: ASEAN is the working proof-of-concept for agenda-setting by the non-great powers — RCEP-anchored trade flows are a hedge against U.S.-centric supply chains.
insights.locator: ASEAN, for example, has turned U.S.-Chinese geopolitical and economic competition

insights.claim: Over the past year many non-great-power countries including Argentina, Ecuador, Malaysia, Paraguay, Peru and the Philippines have explored or signed mineral agreements with the United States, and states holding strategic locations or critical materials should exploit that leverage to advance interests and enshrine norms in bilateral accords.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: A named pipeline of U.S. bilateral minerals deals — the concrete channel for critical-minerals supply diversification and for equity exposure in those jurisdictions.
insights.locator: At the same time, smaller states must become more sophisticated at transactional diplomacy

insights.claim: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has described the current moment as 'the end of a pleasant fiction and the beginning of a harsh reality,' a shift that hits smaller states hardest but does not leave them powerless.
insights.speaker: Tom Long
insights.so_what: A sitting G7 leader framing the order's collapse as settled fact signals allied policy is being rebuilt on that assumption — expect defense and autonomy spending to follow.
insights.quote: the end of a pleasant fiction and the beginning of a harsh reality
insights.locator: What Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has called
